ideas.name: Recruit Reel
ideas.pitch: College-recruiting highlight films and athlete profiles for high-school athletes, filmed at their games and delivered in 72 hours.
ideas.problem: Most of the ~8M US high-school athletes never get seen by college coaches. Recruiting services charge $1,000–$4,000+, and parents film shaky sideline clips that coaches skip after 10 seconds.
ideas.customer: Parents of sophomore–senior athletes in football, soccer, basketball, lacrosse, volleyball and baseball who hope to play in college (D1–D3, NAIA, JUCO).
ideas.how: Film 2–3 games with a phone on an auto-tracking gimbal. Cut a 3–4 minute reel with the athlete's best plays first, spotlight arrows, stats overlay and contact card. Add a one-page web profile (measurables, GPA, schedule, video) and a coach-email template list.
ideas.pricing: Reel $249 · Reel + profile + coach-email kit $449 · Season plan (4 updates) $799
ideas.unit_economics: ≈$449 average order, ≈$25 cost (storage, music license, gas), ≈6 hours of work → ≈$70/hour and 94% gross margin
ideas.startup_cost: $350–$700: auto-tracking phone gimbal, tripod, CapCut/DaVinci (free), a $12/yr domain, Google Forms
ideas.time_to_first_dollar: 1–2 weeks (film a teammate free, post the reel, sell the next one)
ideas.year1: $8K–$30K (20–60 families). Word of mouth inside teams is powerful because every reel is visible to the whole roster.
ideas.moat: A portfolio of reels in one school district, relationships with coaches who refer families, and turnaround speed. Big platforms sell software; you sell a finished product made in person.
risks: Families who think a free phone clip is enough
Never promise a scholarship; promise exposure only
first_steps: Make 3 free reels for teammates and post them with permission
Build a one-page site with pricing and a booking form
Ask every club and HS coach for a 2-minute intro at a parent meeting
ideas.teen_note: Fully teen-doable: you're already at the games. A parent handles payments and contracts.
ideas.why_now: Coaches now recruit from video first. Auto-tracking gimbals cost under $200, so pro-looking footage no longer needs a camera crew.

ideas.name: Ref Ready
ideas.pitch: A referee staffing service for youth rec leagues: certified teen and adult refs booked, scheduled and paid through one simple system.
ideas.problem: Youth leagues across the US are canceling games because of referee shortages, and league volunteers spend hours every week filling slots by text.
ideas.customer: Rec and club leagues (soccer, basketball, flag football), tournament directors and schools' intramural programs.
ideas.how: Recruit and certify local teens (many sports certify refs from age 12–14). Leagues post games; Ref Ready fills them, sends reminders, handles no-shows and collects one invoice. Add mentoring for new refs to reduce dropout.
ideas.pricing: League pays the normal ref fee + a $5–$8 booking fee per game slot · Tournament packages
ideas.unit_economics: A league with 60 games per weekend × $6 ≈ $360/weekend for scheduling work; you can also ref games yourself ($25–$50 each)
ideas.startup_cost: $100–$400 (your certification, a scheduling tool, a simple site)
ideas.moat: Pool of reliable certified refs and league contracts; switching costs once a league runs on your schedule.
risks: Abuse from parents toward young refs; insist on a league code of conduct
Payroll/tax handling (refs are usually independent contractors; a parent handles this)
Certification rules vary by sport and state
first_steps: Get certified yourself and ref this season
Recruit 10 certified friends
Offer one league a free month of scheduling
ideas.teen_note: Ideal: teens are the supply. A parent handles contracts and payouts.
ideas.why_now: Referee shortages are widespread after the pandemic, and leagues will pay to never chase refs again.

ideas.name: Glow Holiday Lights
ideas.pitch: Design, install, take down and store holiday lights for homes and small businesses: one booking, zero ladders for the customer.
ideas.problem: Families want a beautiful house for the holidays but hate ladders, tangles, burnt bulbs and January takedown.
ideas.customer: Busy homeowners in $400K+ neighborhoods, HOAs, restaurants and storefronts.
ideas.how: Measure the roofline from photos, quote commercial-grade LED C9s cut to fit, install in November, maintain through the season, then take down, label and store in January. Next year is a one-click rebooking.
ideas.pricing: Average home $900–$2,000 (lights included year 1) · Renewal ~60% of year 1 · Storage $50/yr
ideas.unit_economics: ≈$1,200 ticket; ≈$350 lights (reused 3+ seasons) + ≈$100 clips/labor → 60–70% margin year 1 and 80%+ on renewals
ideas.startup_cost: $1,500–$3,000: ladders, safety harness, starter light inventory, insurance (parent-held)
ideas.moat: Stored, pre-cut custom lights mean customers rarely switch. Renewal rates in this industry run very high.
risks: Roof and ladder safety: an adult must do anything above one story; teens do ground-level work, design, sales
first_steps: Decorate your own house and 2 neighbors' at cost; photograph at dusk
Flyer streets with the best-lit houses in October
Pre-sell with a 20% deposit by Oct 31
ideas.teen_note: Best as a parent-teen team: the adult handles roofs, you handle design, sales, ground work and the customer list.
ideas.why_now: Commercial LED strings now last 5+ seasons, so year-2 margins are almost pure profit.

ideas.name: Scoop Squad
ideas.pitch: Weekly dog-waste removal subscriptions: boring, unglamorous and very profitable.
ideas.problem: Nobody wants to do it; dog owners would pay to never think about it.
ideas.how: Weekly visits, gates logged in an app, before/after photo texted. Upsell deodorizing.
ideas.moat: Recurring subscriptions are sticky; route density.
first_steps: Flyer 200 homes with visible dogs
First visit free
Referral credit
ideas.why_now: Pet ownership hit record highs, and owners pay for convenience.

ideas.name: Slab Club
ideas.pitch: A trading-card grading concierge: collectors drop off cards; you pre-screen, batch-submit to PSA/SGC/BGS at bulk rates and return slabbed cards.
ideas.problem: Grading is confusing and expensive for casual collectors. They overpay on single submissions and send cards that will grade poorly.
ideas.customer: Sports, Pokémon and TCG collectors, card-shop customers, parents of young collectors.
ideas.how: Collect cards at shops and meetups. Inspect centering, corners and surface under a loupe and light box; reject likely low grades. Pool cards into bulk submissions to cut per-card cost, track every card online and return slabs.
ideas.pricing: $10–$15 per card on top of the grading fee · Pre-screen only $2/card · Sell-on-consignment option 10%
ideas.unit_economics: ≈$12 fee × 100 cards per batch = $1,200 a batch for ≈8 hours of work plus shipping/insurance ≈$60
ideas.startup_cost: $200–$500: loupe, light box, sleeves/top-loaders, a grading-company membership, shipping insurance
ideas.time_to_first_dollar: 2–4 weeks (first batch return takes longer; fees are collected up front)
ideas.moat: Trust plus a track record of grade predictions. Publish your pre-screen accuracy.
risks: Loss or damage in shipping (insure everything)
Liability for high-value cards; cap the declared value at first
first_steps: Grade 20 of your own cards to learn the process
Partner with one local card shop for counter space
Post before/after grade results publicly
ideas.teen_note: A parent co-signs the grading account and insurance. Everything else is teen-run.
ideas.why_now: Card collecting stayed big after the 2020–21 boom, and grading companies keep restructuring prices, which rewards experts who batch.

ideas.name: SetUp Concierge
ideas.pitch: Tech setup and monthly check-ins for seniors: phones, TVs, smart doorbells, video calls, scam protection.
ideas.problem: Seniors struggle with new devices and are top targets for scams; their adult children live far away.
ideas.customer: Seniors and their adult children (often the buyers), plus retirement communities.
ideas.how: Home visits to set up devices, write a personal one-page guide, then a monthly check-in visit or call. Add scam-awareness sessions at community centers.
ideas.moat: Trust and referrals inside retirement communities.
risks: Privacy and liability (never handle passwords for banks)
first_steps: Help 3 neighbors free and collect testimonials
Talk to a retirement community's activities director
Sell the membership to adult children
ideas.teen_note: Ideal for teens: patience and tech skills are the product.
ideas.why_now: The 65+ population is the fastest-growing group, and so are scam losses.

ideas.name: Curbside
ideas.pitch: Weekly trash-bin valet plus monthly bin washing: bins out to the curb, back in, and smelling clean, on subscription.
ideas.problem: Seniors, busy families and people who travel forget bin day, and dirty bins attract pests.
ideas.customer: Seniors, busy families, vacation homes and HOAs.
ideas.how: Route-based weekly service on trash day; monthly bin wash with a pressure washer and eco-safe deodorizer.
ideas.unit_economics: Dense routes: 40 homes in 2 hours ≈ $1,000/month for ≈8 hours/month
risks: Low ticket size; you need density
first_steps: Sign up your own street with door hangers
Offer the HOA a bulk rate
Add washing as an upsell after 30 days
ideas.why_now: Aging population and busy dual-income households.

ideas.name: Gear Library
ideas.pitch: A size-up subscription for kids' sports equipment: hockey, lacrosse, skates and cleats swapped for the next size every season.
ideas.problem: Kids outgrow $300+ of gear every year; parents keep buying new or hunting through used listings.
ideas.customer: Families with kids aged 5–14 in gear-heavy sports.
ideas.how: Families subscribe per kid per sport. They get sanitized, inspected gear in the right size; return it when outgrown and get the next size. Inventory comes from trade-ins and bulk buys.
ideas.unit_economics: A $200 kit rented 3+ seasons at $120 → 80%+ margin after year 1
ideas.moat: Inventory depth across sizes and club partnerships, which are hard to copy quickly.
first_steps: Collect outgrown gear from your own club
Pilot with 10 families in one sport
Partner with the club for a discount
ideas.teen_note: Teen-run with a parent for storage and payments.
ideas.why_now: Youth sports costs keep rising; parents want circular options.

ideas.name: Yard Card
ideas.pitch: Overnight celebration lawn signs for birthdays, graduations, signing days and "welcome home": set up before sunrise, gone in 24 hours.
ideas.problem: Parents want a big, photo-worthy surprise without buying and storing giant decorations.
ideas.customer: Parents in your area, schools (senior signs), teams (signing day), real-estate agents (sold signs).
ideas.how: Own a library of corrugated letters, numbers and graphics. Customer picks a theme online; you set up overnight and collect the next day.
ideas.pricing: $95–$175 per display · School senior-sign packages $25/sign × class size
ideas.unit_economics: ≈$125 per rental, ≈$5 gas, ≈1 hour → ~95% margin once inventory is paid off (often after 6–8rentals)
ideas.startup_cost: $600–$1,200 for the first letter/graphic set and stakes
ideas.moat: Local brand + school contracts; inventory and booking calendar are easy to copy, but relationships aren't.
first_steps: Buy one set, do your sibling's birthday, post it
Pitch the senior class sponsor on graduation signs
List on local Facebook groups and Nextdoor
ideas.teen_note: Excellent teen fit: light, fast, local. A parent drives until you can.
ideas.why_now: Social media rewards photo-worthy moments, and the signs are now cheap to print.

ideas.name: Formal Closet
ideas.pitch: A rental closet for prom, homecoming and winter formal: dresses, suits and accessories at 20% of retail, with fitting nights at your house.
ideas.problem: Teens spend $200–$600 on outfits worn once. Big rental platforms rarely serve teen sizes or local timing.
ideas.customer: High-school students and parents, starting with 3–5 local schools.
ideas.how: Buy inventory cheaply (donations, end-of-season sales, thrift), then host fitting nights before each dance. Rent with a deposit and professional cleaning.
ideas.moat: Peer network inside schools; inventory curated to local trends.
first_steps: Run a donation drive with Student Council
Host the first fitting night before homecoming
Instagram lookbook
ideas.teen_note: Excellent teen fit; it lives inside your school's social network.
ideas.why_now: Sustainability is a strong value for Gen Z, and resale apps proved teens accept pre-owned fashion.

ideas.name: FLOW Edge
ideas.pitch: A skate-sharpening and gear-freshening subscription for youth hockey families, picked up after practice and returned before the next one.
ideas.problem: Pro-shop trips and dull skates waste family time.
ideas.customer: Youth hockey and figure-skating families at one rink.
ideas.how: Team pickup, a consumer automatic sharpener, a sharpening log and reminders.
ideas.unit_economics: ≈5 minutes per pair; 90% margin on sharpening
first_steps: Sharpen 50 pairs free for practice
Confirm the rink's policy
Pilot with one team
ideas.teen_note: Teen-run; a parent buys the machine.
ideas.why_now: Consumer automatic sharpeners made pro-level sharpening portable.

ideas.name: Snapbooth
ideas.pitch: A sleek iPad photo booth for parties, proms, bar mitzvahs and corporate events, with instant texted GIFs and branded prints.
ideas.problem: Professional booths cost $600–$1,500 a night. Smaller events want the fun without the price.
ideas.customer: Party hosts, school dances, quinceañeras, small businesses, real-estate open houses.
ideas.how: iPad booth app (e.g. a subscription booth app), ring light, backdrop, props, optional dye-sub printer. Guests text themselves photos and GIFs; host gets a gallery.
ideas.unit_economics: ≈$350 per event, ≈$40 consumables/app, ≈5 hours including setup → 85%+ margin
ideas.startup_cost: $900–$2,000 (iPad you may already own, stand, light, backdrop, props)
risks: Competition from cheap rentals; win on looks and service
first_steps: Run it free at a friend's party, collect video testimonials
Partner with 2 local DJs for referrals
Offer schools a prom package
ideas.teen_note: Teen-run at events; a parent co-signs bookings and drives gear.
ideas.why_now: Instant sharing made booths more social. Venues love them as add-ons.

ideas.name: Move-Out Rescue
ideas.pitch: Collect furniture students abandon at college move-out (free or cheap) and resell it to incoming students at move-in, delivered.
ideas.problem: Thousands of mini-fridges, desks and couches get dumped every May while new students buy the same items in August.
ideas.customer: Graduating students (supply) and incoming freshmen and their parents (demand).
ideas.how: Arrange free pickups in May, store in a rented unit, sell move-in bundles online in August with delivery.
ideas.unit_economics: Items acquired near $0; storage ≈$150/month for 3 months; 100 items ≈ $8K–$12K revenue
ideas.moat: Relationships with campus housing and student groups.
first_steps: Pick one nearby college
Contact housing and sustainability offices
Pre-sell bundles to incoming students on parent Facebook groups
ideas.teen_note: A parent drives and rents the storage. Teens run sourcing, listings and sales.
ideas.why_now: Universities want less move-out waste, and sustainability offices partner readily.

ideas.name: Memory Lane
ideas.pitch: Local pickup of old photos, slides and home videos, digitized, organized by year and delivered in a private online album plus a USB drive.
ideas.problem: Boxes of VHS tapes and photos are decaying in closets; mail-away services feel risky.
ideas.customer: Grandparents and parents, plus families preparing anniversaries or memorials.
ideas.how: Pickup in person, scan photos with a high-speed scanner, capture tapes with a VHS-to-USB device, auto-enhance, organize by date and deliver.
ideas.pricing: $0.40–$0.60 per photo · $25–$35 per tape · Memorial slideshow $150
ideas.unit_economics: A typical order (1,000 photos + 10 tapes) ≈ $800 for ≈12 hours of mostly machine time
ideas.startup_cost: $700–$1,500 (fast photo scanner, capture device, VCR, storage)
ideas.moat: Trust (local, in-person) beats mail-away; reviews from seniors spread through churches and community centers.
first_steps: Digitize your own family's albums
Offer a demo at a senior center
Holiday-gift campaign in November
ideas.teen_note: Excellent teen fit; work from home.
ideas.why_now: Original media is now 30–60 years old and degrading.

ideas.name: Tourney Base
ideas.pitch: A tournament-day basecamp for youth sports families: canopy, chairs, cooler, charging and snacks set up before the first game.
ideas.problem: All-day tournaments mean hauling gear across huge complexes in heat or rain.
ideas.customer: Families and teams at travel tournaments.
ideas.how: Teams book per weekend; you set up a branded basecamp near their field and take it down at the end of the day.
ideas.pricing: $300–$500 per team per tournament day · Snack add-ons
ideas.unit_economics: $400 per team; ≈$60 costs; 2 teams per staffer per day
first_steps: Do it free for your own team once
Pitch the tournament director on vendor status
Sell to team managers, not parents
ideas.teen_note: Teen crew with a parent supervising and driving.
ideas.why_now: Travel sports is a $30B+ industry and families spend heavily on convenience.

red_team.name: Recruit Reel
attacks: Why would customers refuse?
Free tools exist (phone + editing apps), and big recruiting services already sell to these families.
Why hasn't this already won?
National services sell software and email blasts, not in-person filming at local games. Local videographers charge $1,000+ and are slow.
Could competitors copy it?
Yes, but the moat is local presence, speed, and a visible portfolio inside each team.
Is the market large enough?
One high school has ~300 varsity athletes; even 5% buying at $449 is about $6.7K per school per year.
Is pricing realistic?
Yes: well under recruiting services ($1K–$4K) and higher-value than a shaky clip.
Can a teenager execute it?
Yes: you're already at games, editing skills are learnable in weeks, and the gear is under $500.
Legal issues
Filming minors needs parent consent; use licensed music; NCAA rules allow third-party highlight videos. Never promise scholarships.
Operational bottleneck
Editing time in peak season. Fix: templates, a standard reel structure, and hiring a second editor.
Killer assumption
Parents will pay before seeing results. Mitigation: free 30-second teaser from the first game.
red_team.fix: Lead with a free teaser, sell the $449 package, and add season updates for recurring revenue. Build a coach-email tracker to prove exposure (opens and replies).

red_team.name: Ref Ready
attacks: Why would leagues refuse?
Some assignors already do this as volunteers or through assigning software.
Killer assumption
You can keep enough reliable refs. Teen refs quit mostly because of parent abuse, so mentoring and conduct rules are the product.
Copyable?
Assigning software exists. The moat is your pool of refs and the league relationship.
Legal
Contractor payments, certification requirements and youth work rules. A parent runs payouts.
red_team.fix: Start as a ref yourself, then add scheduling for one league. Charge per filled slot and guarantee coverage with a backup list.

red_team.name: Glow Holiday Lights
attacks: Killer assumption
A teen can safely do roof installs. They can't alone: adult handles all elevated work.
Seasonality
90% of revenue in 10 weeks. Fine as a high-earning winter season.
Copyable?
Easily, but stored custom-cut lights create high renewal lock-in.
Legal
Liability insurance and adult ownership required.
red_team.fix: Parent-teen company. Ground-level and single-story homes first; upsell permanent track lighting via an installer partner for referral fees.

method: Each idea is scored 1–10 on 11 criteria, with 'Low cost' and 'Teen-able' scored so higher is better. The FLOW score weights earning power: profit ×2, demand and long-term ×1.5, scalability ×1.3, recurring ×1.2, speed ×0.8, the rest ×1. Earnings ranges are estimates for a part-time teen operator with parental help; verify local prices.
